Content:
For this reason, it's often more helpful to give a range of possible values for [MATH: \mu.] In other words, instead of reporting a single estimate [MATH: \overline{x},] we might instead report a so-called confidence interval, which is an interval of the form

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the distribution of sample mean is also normal, and we have that

[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim N(0,1),]

where

  • [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,

  • [MATH: \mu] is the population mean,

  • [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance, and

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] of the original distribution is given by

[MATH: \overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.05} = 1.645.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is the following:

[MATH: − 5 ± 1.645 ⋅ (2)/(sqrt(9)); − 5 ± 1.097]

sections.normalized_html:
Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=196] from a population with standard deviation [MATH: \sigma=7.] Given that the mean of the sample is [MATH: \overline{x}=24,] find a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] of the distribution.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.96) = 0.025,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram below.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We do not know the distribution of the population. However, the sample size [MATH: n = 196 \geq 30] is sufficiently large. Therefore, according to the central limit theorem, we may use the following approximation: [MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim N(0,1),]

where

  • [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,

  • [MATH: \mu] is the population mean,

  • [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance, and

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] of the original distribution is given by

[MATH: \overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.96) = 0.025.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.025} = 1.96.]

Therefore, the [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is the following:

[MATH: 24 ± 1.96 ⋅ (7)/(sqrt(196)); 24 ± 0.98]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we conduct a random sample of size [MATH: n=10] from a normal population with the unknown population mean [MATH: \mu] and known population variance [MATH: \sigma^2=9.] After processing our results, we compute the mean of this sample using the usual methods and get the following result:

Content:
[MATH: \overline{x}=12]

Content:
This is an unbiased estimate of the population mean [MATH: \mu.] However, it is unsatisfactory because we have no information regarding its reliability.

Content:
For this reason, it's often more helpful to give a range of possible values for [MATH: \mu.] In other words, instead of reporting a single estimate [MATH: \overline{x},] we might instead report a so-called confidence interval, which is an interval of the form

Content:
[MATH: (\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E)]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \overline{x}] is our estimate of the population mean, and
- [MATH: E] is some margin of error.

Content:
In addition, we need to give some indication regarding the reliability of our confidence interval. With this in mind, we will construct a [MATH: \boldsymbol{95\%}] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu]. The precise meaning of this will become clear shortly.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Constructing Confidence Intervals

Content:
In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] is also normally distributed, where

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Content:
By transforming [MATH: \overline{X}] to a standard normal random variable, we have

Content:
[MATH: Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1).]

Content:
We wish to find a [MATH: z]-interval that we're [MATH: 95\%] confident that the random variable [MATH: Z] lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ecd56581880a6de7bcb44b1b91bca82b]

Content:
To help with the notation, we define a new parameter [MATH: \alpha.] Since we're computing a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval, we have

Content:
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as [MATH: \pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c975f51fe63c7b103c70a4ef3e8ff7bf]

Content:
According to our diagram,

Content:
[MATH: P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.]

Content:
Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that [MATH: z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
[MATH: P(− 1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95.]

Content:
Therefore, there is a [MATH: 95\%] probability that our random variable [MATH: Z] will lie in the interval [MATH: (-1.96, 1.96).]

Content:
Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean [MATH: \mu\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: − 1.96 <|Z < 1.96; − 1.96 <|(x^(―) − μ)/(σ/sqrt(n)) < 1.96; − 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)) <|x^(―) − μ < 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)); − x^(―) − 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)) <|− μ < − x^(―) + 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)); x^(―) + 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)) >|μ > x^(―) − 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)); x^(―) − 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)) <|μ < x^(―) + 1.96 ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n))]

Content:
Therefore, a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)]

Content:
Finally, substituting our values

Content:
[MATH: n=10, \qquad
\overline{x}=12, \qquad
\sigma=3,]

Content:
we obtain that our [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for [MATH: \mu] is

Content:
[MATH: \big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).]

Content:
Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Known Population Variance

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a normal population with the unknown population mean [MATH: \mu] and known population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Then, for a given value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)]

Content:
where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
The endpoints of our confidence interval are called confidence limits and are given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.]

Content:
Each part of the formula above has a name:

Content:
- [MATH: \overline{x}] is an estimate of the population mean
- [MATH: \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}] is the standard error of the mean
- [MATH: z_{\alpha/2}] is the corresponding [MATH: z]-score
- [MATH: E = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}] is the margin of error

Content:
[MATH: z]

Content:
So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (x^(―) − [margin of error],|x^(―) + [margin of error]); (x^(―) − [[math]z[/math]-score] ⋅ [standard error],|x^(―) + [[math]z[/math]-score] ⋅ [standard error]); (x^(―) − z_{α/2} ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)),|x^(―) + z_{α/2} ⋅ (σ)/(sqrt(n)))]

Content:
Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably.

---

Item 4 — Example: Finding Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations

Example Prompt:

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/a34a5cb32ea4e02e915cb8d65c01bcb2]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are told that the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the distribution of sample mean is also normal, and we have that

[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim N(0,1),]

where

- [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,
- [MATH: \mu] is the population mean,
- [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance, and
- [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] of the original distribution is given by

[MATH: \overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.05} = 1.645.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is the following:

[MATH: − 5 ± 1.645 ⋅ (2)/(sqrt(9)); − 5 ± 1.097]

Item 7 — Tutorial: Interpreting Confidence Intervals

Content:
It's important to be able to interpret confidence intervals correctly.

Content:
Imagine we conduct several independent random samples from a population. The mean of the sample will be different for each sample. Some values of [MATH: \overline{x}] might lie close to the population mean [MATH: \mu,] and some could lie further away.

Content:
Suppose we construct a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for each sample and plot them on the same diagram. We might get a picture similar to the one below.

Content:

Content:
